concepts.title: AWS Global Infrastructure and the Shared Responsibility Model
concepts.description: AWS's physical infrastructure is organized into Regions and Availability Zones, and understanding that geography is what makes multi-AZ redundancy meaningful; the Shared Responsibility Model then draws the line between what AWS secures and what you must secure yourself.
learningObjectives: Explain the relationship between Regions, Availability Zones, and data centers, and why AZs are physically isolated from each other.
Explain why deploying resources across multiple AZs -- not just multiple servers in one AZ -- is what actually provides fault tolerance.
State the Shared Responsibility Model's dividing line and explain how it shifts between IaaS (EC2), managed services (RDS), and serverless (Lambda, S3).
Given a described security incident, identify whether it falls under AWS's responsibility or the customer's.
Explain why choosing a Region involves latency, compliance/data-residency, and pricing trade-offs, not just picking 'the closest one.'

sections.heading: Regions: Independent, Isolated Geographic Areas
sections.body:
An AWS Region -- `us-east-1` (Northern Virginia), `eu-west-1` (Ireland), `ap-southeast-2` (Sydney), and so on -- is a distinct geographic area containing its own fully independent, isolated set of AWS infrastructure. Regions do not share data, compute, or state with each other automatically: an EC2 instance you launch in `us-east-1` does not exist, and is not even visible, when you switch your console or CLI to `ap-southeast-1`. This isolation is deliberate, not a limitation. It contains blast radius -- a catastrophic failure or a botched deployment in one Region cannot cascade into another the way it could if everything were secretly one giant shared system. It also lets you satisfy data-residency and compliance requirements (GDPR's rules about where EU citizens' data physically lives, or a contract that requires data to stay within a specific country) simply by choosing which Region to operate in, since a Region is a real commitment about where bytes are stored, not just a label.

Most AWS services are Region-scoped: you pick a Region, and everything you create with that service lives only there, addressed by ARNs that literally embed the Region name (`arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket` is a partial exception since S3 bucket names are globally unique, but the underlying storage still lives in one Region). A smaller set of services are global by design -- IAM (users, roles, and policies aren't tied to any one Region), Route 53 (DNS), and CloudFront (which uses a worldwide network of edge locations, a different and much larger concept than Regions, purely for caching content close to end users). Knowing which category a given service falls into matters the first time you go looking for 'my resource' in the console and can't find it -- nine times out of ten, you're just looking at the wrong Region selector in the top corner.

sections.heading: Availability Zones: Why 'Multiple Servers' Isn't the Same as 'Multiple AZs'
sections.body:
Within a Region, AWS operates multiple Availability Zones (AZs) -- most Regions have three or more. Each AZs is one or more discrete, physically separate data centers, with its own independent power, cooling, and physical network connectivity, typically miles apart from the other AZs in the same Region (far enough that a single flood, fire, or power-grid failure is very unlikely to take out two AZs at once, but close enough that network latency between AZs in the same Region is low, single-digit milliseconds, so splitting a workload across AZs doesn't meaningfully hurt performance).

This is the detail that trips up a lot of people who are new to cloud infrastructure: launching two, three, or ten EC2 instances does *not*, by itself, buy you fault tolerance against anything. If all of those instances live in the same AZ, they still share the same power source, the same cooling system, and the same physical network fabric -- an AZ-level event takes all of them down simultaneously, no matter how many there are. Redundancy only protects you against the failure domain you actually diversify across. Two instances in `us-east-1a` and `us-east-1a` again are not meaningfully redundant against an AZ failure; two instances, one in `us-east-1a` and one in `us-east-1b`, are, because those two AZs don't share the infrastructure that's likely to fail. This is precisely why almost every AWS reference architecture you'll see insists on 'at least two AZs' as a baseline -- it's not a stylistic preference, it's the actual unit that AWS's own infrastructure design makes into an independent failure domain.

sections.heading: The Shared Responsibility Model: 'Security OF the Cloud' vs 'Security IN the Cloud'
sections.body:
AWS frames its security obligations with a single, deliberately memorable split: AWS is responsible for the security **of** the cloud, and the customer is responsible for security **in** the cloud. 'Of the cloud' covers everything AWS itself owns and operates and that you have no visibility into or control over: the physical security of data centers, the durability of the underlying storage hardware, the integrity of the network backbone, and the hypervisor layer that isolates one customer's virtual machines from another's on shared physical hosts. 'In the cloud' covers everything you build on top of that: which guest-OS patches you've applied to your EC2 instances, what your application code does, whether your data is encrypted and with which keys, whether your IAM policies are correctly scoped, and whether your S3 bucket policies and security groups only allow the access you intended.

Where exactly that line falls shifts depending on how much of the stack a given service manages for you. With EC2 (infrastructure-as-a-service), you're responsible for the guest operating system, its patches, and everything above it -- AWS only guarantees the physical host and hypervisor. With a managed service like RDS, AWS also takes over patching the underlying OS and the database engine itself, though you still fully own access control (IAM, security groups, database credentials) and the correctness of your own data and queries. With something like S3 or Lambda, AWS manages nearly the entire stack -- you're mostly left responsible for how you configure access to what you store or run, and what you actually put in it.

This distinction is not academic. Look at almost any widely reported 'AWS data breach' from the last decade and you'll find, on close inspection, that it wasn't AWS's infrastructure that failed -- it was a customer-created S3 bucket left publicly readable, or an IAM policy far broader than intended, or an access key accidentally committed to a public GitHub repo. Those are squarely on the 'in the cloud' side of the line, and no amount of AWS's own infrastructure hardening protects against them, because they aren't infrastructure failures at all -- they're configuration mistakes made by the customer, using tools AWS provided correctly.

sections.heading: Choosing a Region: Latency, Compliance, and Price Are Different Axes
sections.body:
Picking 'the Region closest to me' is a reasonable default, but it's only one of several independent factors that actually matter, and treating it as the only one leads to real problems later. Latency to your users is one legitimate axis -- physical distance and network hops translate directly into round-trip time, which matters a lot for interactive applications and much less for a nightly batch job. Compliance and data residency is a second, entirely separate axis -- some regulations (GDPR-adjacent rules in the EU, data sovereignty laws in several countries) require certain categories of data to physically remain within a specific jurisdiction, which can force a Region choice that has nothing to do with where your engineering team or even your users are located. Price is a third axis, genuinely independent of the other two -- Regions are not priced identically for the same instance type or storage class, and `us-east-1`, being AWS's oldest and largest Region, is very often (though not always) among the cheapest. A fourth, easy-to-forget axis is service availability itself: brand-new AWS services and features frequently launch in `us-east-1` first and roll out to other Regions over subsequent months, so a Region choice made purely for latency or compliance reasons can quietly limit which services you're even able to use.

It's also worth being precise about scope: everything above is about choosing *a* Region to operate in, which is a different (and much more involved, and much more expensive) decision than architecting for *multiple* Regions simultaneously for disaster recovery. Multi-AZ, within a single Region, is treated as the normal baseline expectation for any production workload that cares about availability at all. Multi-Region is a substantial additional undertaking -- data replication across Regions is neither instant nor free, and most teams reach for it only when a single Region's worst-case outage genuinely isn't an acceptable risk for the business, not as a routine default.

examples.title: Listing a Region's Availability Zones with the AWS CLI
examples.code:
aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --region us-east-1 --query "AvailabilityZones[].{Name:ZoneName,Id:ZoneId,State:State}" --output table

# -------------------------------------------------
# |            DescribeAvailabilityZones           |
# +-----------+---------------+---------------------+
# |    Id     |     Name      |        State        |
# +-----------+---------------+---------------------+
# |  use1-az1 |  us-east-1a   |  available           |
# |  use1-az2 |  us-east-1b   |  available           |
# |  use1-az4 |  us-east-1d   |  available           |
# |  use1-az6 |  us-east-1f   |  available           |
# +-----------+---------------+---------------------+
examples.explanation: This calls the EC2 API directly to list every Availability Zone AWS has provisioned for your account in `us-east-1`, along with a stable Zone ID (`use1-az1`) next to the more familiar Zone Name (`us-east-1a`). The Zone ID is the detail worth internalizing: AWS deliberately maps the human-readable letter suffixes (`a`, `b`, `c`...) to different physical AZs for different AWS accounts, specifically to spread customer load evenly across AZs rather than having everyone's 'first' instance pile into the same physical `-a` zone. That means `us-east-1a` in your account is not necessarily the same physical data center as `us-east-1a` in someone else's account -- if you ever need a stable identifier for cross-account AZ coordination (for example, making sure two accounts' subnets in 'the same AZ' really are physically co-located for latency reasons), use the Zone ID, not the letter suffix.

examples.title: Same Deployment, Two Different Failure Domains
examples.code:
# Single-AZ: both instances launched into the same subnet -> the same AZ
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abcd1234 --instance-type t3.micro \
  --subnet-id subnet-aaa111 --count 2   # subnet-aaa111 lives entirely in us-east-1a

# Multi-AZ: one instance per subnet, each subnet in a different AZ
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abcd1234 --instance-type t3.micro \
  --subnet-id subnet-aaa111 --count 1   # us-east-1a
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0abcd1234 --instance-type t3.micro \
  --subnet-id subnet-bbb222 --count 1   # us-east-1b
examples.explanation: The two `run-instances` calls in the first block look perfectly reasonable -- two instances, presumably for redundancy -- but because both are launched into `subnet-aaa111`, and a subnet is permanently pinned to exactly one AZ at creation time, both instances end up physically in `us-east-1a`. If that AZ has a power or network event, both instances go down together; the count of two bought no protection against that specific failure mode at all (it would still help against, say, one instance simply crashing on its own). The second block launches the same total capacity but spreads it across two subnets that live in two different AZs. Now an `us-east-1a` outage leaves the `us-east-1b` instance running -- the redundancy is real because it lines up with an actual independent failure domain, not just a higher instance count.

examples.title: Shared Responsibility in Practice: A Public S3 Bucket
examples.explanation: This is a bucket policy someone attached to `customer-exports-bucket`, almost certainly intending to grant read access to some specific application or account. The `"Principal": "*"` with no `Condition` clause instead grants `s3:GetObject` to literally anyone on the internet who can guess or discover an object's key -- and object keys for exported customer data files are exactly the kind of thing that ends up indexed by search engines or leaked through a misconfigured link. Notice what AWS is *not* at fault for here: the underlying storage engine correctly and durably stored every byte exactly as instructed, the hardware didn't fail, the region and AZ redundancy behind S3 worked flawlessly. The failure is entirely in how a customer configured access to a resource they created -- squarely on the 'security in the cloud' side of the shared responsibility line. This is why AWS ships tools like S3 Block Public Access and IAM Access Analyzer as safety nets, but stops short of silently overriding a policy you explicitly wrote; the responsibility to write it correctly is yours.

misconceptions.description: If I launch multiple EC2 instances for my application, it's automatically fault-tolerant against infrastructure failures.
misconceptions.clarification: Fault tolerance comes from diversifying across independent failure domains, not merely from having more than one instance. If every instance lives in the same Availability Zone, they all share the same power, cooling, and physical network -- an AZ-level event takes all of them down together regardless of count. Real fault tolerance against an AZ failure requires spreading instances across at least two AZs (which in turn requires at least two subnets, since a subnet is pinned to one AZ), typically behind a load balancer that can route around whichever AZ is currently unhealthy.

misconceptions.description: Because AWS is responsible for 'security of the cloud,' AWS will notice and fix things like an overly permissive IAM policy or a publicly readable S3 bucket that I configured.
misconceptions.clarification: AWS's side of the shared responsibility line covers the physical infrastructure, hardware, network backbone, and hypervisor -- not the correctness of resources and permissions you configure on top of that infrastructure. A misconfigured bucket policy or an overly broad IAM policy is a customer-side ('in the cloud') responsibility; AWS provides tools such as IAM Access Analyzer and S3 Block Public Access to help you find and prevent these mistakes, but it does not take over the responsibility of getting your own configuration right, and it generally will not silently override a policy you explicitly and validly wrote.

exercises.prompt: A team deployed two EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer, believing this made their service resilient to an Availability Zone outage. Below is a simplified view of the deployment. Find the reliability bug and fix it.
hints: Count how many genuinely distinct Availability Zones actually appear across the two instances -- not how many instances there are.
The load balancer itself is only attached to one subnet here too -- that's a second, separate instance of the same underlying problem, not a different bug.
A subnet is permanently tied to exactly one AZ, so fixing this requires introducing a second subnet that lives in a different AZ, and using it for both an instance and the load balancer.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Both instances originally lived in `subnet-0f1e2d3c`, which is pinned to `us-east-1a` -- so despite there being two instances, there was only one real failure domain, and an `us-east-1a` outage would have taken both down simultaneously. The load balancer was in the same position, attached to only that one subnet. The fix moves the second instance into a new subnet, `subnet-0a9b8c7d`, that lives in `us-east-1b`, and adds that subnet to the load balancer's subnet list as well (in practice, AWS actually requires an Application Load Balancer to be associated with subnets in at least two AZs before it can even be created, precisely to prevent this exact single-AZ trap). Now an `us-east-1a` failure leaves the `us-east-1b` instance -- and the load balancer's path to it -- fully intact.

exercises.prompt: A company runs production EC2 instances split across three Availability Zones in one Region, behind a multi-AZ Application Load Balancer, with its data stored in S3 (which AWS replicates across multiple AZs within the Region automatically as part of the service). One Availability Zone in that Region suffers a power failure. Describe what happens to (a) the EC2 instances in the failed AZ, (b) the EC2 instances in the other two AZs, and (c) the S3 data, and explain why each behaves that way.
hints: Treat each AWS resource by asking whether it is tied to one specific AZ or spread across/managed independently of any single AZ.
The ALB continuously health-checks every registered instance -- what does it do with instances that stop responding?
S3 objects are not launched into a specific AZ the way an EC2 instance is; think about how the durability guarantee described for S3 is actually implemented.
exercises.expectedAnswer: (a) i-1, physically located in us-east-1a, becomes unreachable and effectively fails along with the rest of that AZ's power and network infrastructure. (b) i-2 and i-3, in us-east-1b and us-east-1c, are unaffected, since they run on independent power, cooling, and network infrastructure; the ALB's health checks detect that i-1 has stopped responding, mark it unhealthy, and stop routing new traffic to it, continuing to serve all traffic from i-2 and i-3. (c) The S3 data in the app-data bucket remains fully available and intact, because S3 (unlike an EC2 instance, which is launched into and stays tied to one specific AZ) stores object data redundantly across multiple AZs within the Region as an intrinsic part of how the service itself works, not as something the customer had to configure.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This scenario isolates the difference between AZ-pinned resources and Region-scoped, AWS-managed redundancy. EC2 instances are provisioned into a specific subnet, and a subnet lives in exactly one AZ -- so i-1 genuinely goes down with its AZ, with no automatic recovery of that specific instance. The ALB's job is precisely to paper over exactly this kind of partial failure: its health checks are running continuously in the background regardless of whether anything has gone wrong, so the moment i-1 stops responding, it's excluded from the routing pool within a couple of failed health-check intervals, and clients simply keep getting served -- now entirely by the two surviving AZs, at reduced total capacity rather than zero capacity. S3 sits in a different category entirely: you never chose an AZ when you created the bucket or wrote an object, because S3's durability design already spreads object data across multiple AZs within the Region behind the scenes as part of the base service -- this is exactly the kind of built-in resilience that the earlier explanation about durability vs. AZ-pinned compute resources is pointing at.

assessments.prompt: A company runs a single EC2 instance in us-east-1a serving production traffic. Which change most directly improves its resilience against an Availability-Zone-level failure?
options: Launch a second, identical EC2 instance also in us-east-1a and register both with a target group.
Resize the existing EC2 instance to a larger instance type, still in us-east-1a.
Launch a second EC2 instance in a different Availability Zone, such as us-east-1b, and place both instances behind a load balancer spanning both AZs.
Migrate the instance to an entirely different AWS Region.
assessments.explanation: AZ-level fault tolerance requires diversifying across independent failure domains -- adding a second instance in the same AZ (option A) doesn't achieve that, since both instances still share the same power, cooling, and network infrastructure and would fail together. Resizing to a bigger instance (option B) addresses capacity or performance, not AZ-level failure, and doesn't touch the underlying single-point-of-failure at all. Migrating Regions entirely (option D) is a disproportionate, much more expensive response to an AZ-level concern, and doesn't by itself provide any redundancy either -- it just relocates the same single point of failure elsewhere. Option C is the direct, standard fix: a second instance in a genuinely different AZ, with a load balancer spanning both, means the failure of either AZ alone leaves the other fully able to serve traffic.

assessments.prompt: The AWS CLI's `describe-availability-zones` output shows both a Zone Name (like `us-east-1a`) and a Zone ID (like `use1-az1`) for each Availability Zone. Why does AWS recommend using the Zone ID rather than the Zone Name for cross-account AZ coordination?
options: Zone IDs are simply a shorter, more convenient alias for Zone Names with no functional difference between accounts.

AWS deliberately maps the letter suffixes in Zone Names to different physical AZs for different accounts, to spread customer load evenly -- so 'us-east-1a' in one account may not be the same physical data center as 'us-east-1a' in another, while the Zone ID stays a stable identifier for the physical AZ.
Zone Names are deprecated and will stop working in a future API version.
Zone IDs are required because Zone Names only work within the AWS Management Console, not the CLI.
assessments.explanation: AWS intentionally randomizes which physical AZ gets labeled 'a', 'b', 'c' and so on per account specifically to avoid everyone's first-launched resources piling into the same physical location -- this means the human-readable Zone Name is account-relative, not a stable physical identifier. The Zone ID (e.g. `use1-az1`) is the stable identifier that does correspond to the same physical AZ across every account, which is exactly why it's the right thing to use when two separate accounts need to confirm their subnets truly sit in the same physical AZ (for example, to guarantee low-latency, same-AZ networking across an account boundary). Options A, C, and D all invent reasons that don't reflect how AWS actually assigns these labels; Zone Names remain fully functional everywhere, they're simply not physically stable across accounts.

assessments.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes how the Shared Responsibility Model's dividing line shifts across EC2, RDS, and Lambda?
options: The dividing line never shifts -- AWS always secures only the physical hardware and hypervisor, and the customer is always responsible for everything above that, regardless of which service is used.

With EC2, the customer patches and secures the guest operating system and everything above it; with RDS, AWS additionally takes over OS and database-engine patching while the customer still owns access control and data; with Lambda, AWS manages nearly the entire stack and the customer is mainly responsible for their code and how they configure access to it.
With Lambda, the customer must still patch the underlying operating system themselves, since AWS never manages OS patching for serverless compute.
With RDS, the customer is responsible for the hypervisor layer, since databases require lower-level hardware access than plain EC2 instances.
assessments.explanation: The Shared Responsibility line moves based on how much of the stack a given service manages on your behalf: EC2 is infrastructure-as-a-service, so AWS only guarantees the physical host and hypervisor while the customer owns the guest OS and up; RDS is a managed service, so AWS additionally absorbs OS and database-engine patching, leaving the customer responsible mainly for access control and their own data and queries; Lambda abstracts away nearly everything, leaving the customer responsible chiefly for their application code and how they've configured access to it. Option A ignores that this line demonstrably does shift between service categories, and options C and D both invert the actual responsibility split for their respective services.

assessments.prompt: Explain the Shared Responsibility Model in your own words, including one concrete example of a security failure that would fall on AWS's side of the line, and one that would fall on the customer's side.
assessments.modelAnswer: The Shared Responsibility Model splits security obligations along the boundary of who actually controls a given layer of the stack. AWS is responsible for 'security of the cloud': the physical security of its data centers, the integrity and durability of the underlying storage and networking hardware, and the hypervisor layer that keeps different customers' workloads properly isolated from one another on shared physical machines -- none of which a customer has any visibility into or ability to configure, so it wouldn't make sense to hold the customer responsible for it. The customer is responsible for 'security in the cloud': everything they configure and build using AWS's building blocks, including which operating system patches they apply to their EC2 instances, how they write and secure their own application code, how they encrypt and handle their own data, and critically, how they configure access control -- IAM policies, security groups, and resource policies like S3 bucket policies. A failure on AWS's side of the line would look like, for example, a flaw in the Nitro hypervisor that let one customer's EC2 instance read another customer's memory -- a failure in infrastructure the customer never had access to and couldn't have prevented. A failure on the customer's side would look like an engineer attaching a bucket policy with `"Principal": "*"` to an S3 bucket containing sensitive exports, making every object in it readable by anyone on the internet -- the storage service itself worked exactly as instructed and never lost or corrupted any data; the mistake was entirely in how a customer-controlled permission was configured. In practice, the overwhelming majority of publicized cloud security incidents fall into this second category, which is exactly why understanding where the line actually sits, rather than assuming AWS's infrastructure security somehow extends to cover your own configuration mistakes, matters so much in practice.

concepts.title: IAM Fundamentals: Users, Roles, and Policies
concepts.description: IAM answers two questions on every single AWS API call -- who is making this request, and what are they allowed to do -- and understanding principals, policies, and especially roles is the foundation for using AWS safely rather than merely functionally.
learningObjectives: Distinguish IAM users, groups, and roles, and explain when each is the appropriate principal to use.
Read and write a basic IAM policy document, identifying Effect, Action, Resource, and Principal.
Explain why an EC2 instance or Lambda function should assume a role rather than have long-lived access keys stored on it.
Explain the principle of least privilege and why wildcards in Action or Resource are a common source of security incidents.
Trace how AWS evaluates multiple applicable policies for a single request, including the rule that an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow.

sections.heading: Principals: Users, Groups, and Roles
sections.body:
Every AWS API call is made by some **principal** -- an identity IAM can recognize and evaluate permissions for. An **IAM user** is a long-lived identity meant for a specific person or application: it can have a console password, and it can have access keys (a static access key ID and secret) for programmatic access. Those credentials don't expire on their own, which is exactly what makes users convenient for humans logging into the console and exactly what makes them risky for anything else, as the next section covers. A **group** is not actually a principal at all -- it's a container you put users into purely so you can attach a policy once and have it apply to every user in the group; you cannot make an API call 'as a group,' and a group can't be referenced as a `Principal` in a trust or resource policy. An **IAM role** is an identity with no permanent credentials of its own -- instead, a trusted principal (a human via federation, an EC2 instance, a Lambda function, another AWS account, or an AWS service) *assumes* the role via AWS's Security Token Service (STS) and receives temporary credentials, typically valid for anywhere from 15 minutes to several hours, after which they expire automatically.

That expiry is the whole point, and it's why roles have become the default recommended principal for essentially anything that isn't literally a human typing a password into the console. A leaked access key from a long-lived user is a static secret that works until someone notices and manually revokes it -- which, in practice, security researchers have shown can be scraped from a public GitHub push and abused within minutes. A leaked temporary credential from an assumed role is only useful for whatever time window remains before it expires on its own, with no manual revocation required. It's also worth explicitly noting the AWS account's **root user**: the single identity created when the account itself was created, which has unrestricted access to everything, cannot be restricted by any IAM policy, and should essentially never be used for day-to-day work -- AWS's own guidance is to secure it with MFA, lock away its credentials, and do all routine work through IAM users and roles instead.

sections.heading: Policies: JSON Documents That Grant or Deny
How AWS Evaluates a Request: Default Deny, and Explicit Deny Always Wins
sections.body:
The evaluation logic behind every single AWS API call follows a small number of fixed rules, and they're worth memorizing precisely because getting them backwards leads to real security incidents. First: everything is denied by default. An action is only permitted if some applicable policy contains an explicit `Allow` for it. Second, and critically: if *any* applicable policy -- an identity-based policy, a resource-based policy, a permissions boundary, or an AWS Organizations Service Control Policy (SCP) -- contains an explicit `Deny` for that action, the request is denied, full stop, no matter how many `Allow` statements exist elsewhere that would otherwise have permitted it. Explicit Deny always wins.

This rule is exactly what makes permission boundaries and SCPs useful as organization-wide guardrails: an administrator can set an SCP that explicitly denies, say, disabling CloudTrail logging or leaving a Region entirely, and no IAM policy any individual account admin writes -- however broad -- can override that. But the same rule bites people in the ordinary, single-account case too. A common real mistake looks like this: someone grants `s3:*` broadly to a role during development (an all-too-common shortcut, covered in the next section), then later tries to lock down just the dangerous parts with a targeted `Deny` on `s3:DeleteBucket` -- but writes the Deny's `Resource` field with a typo or an overly narrow ARN pattern that doesn't actually match the bucket in question. The Deny silently fails to apply where it was needed, and the broad Allow underneath it is left fully in effect. The lesson isn't 'avoid Deny statements' -- it's that a Deny is only as good as its own Resource/Action matching, and it's never a substitute for simply not granting the broad Allow in the first place.

sections.heading: Roles for Machines: Why EC2 Instances Shouldn't Carry Access Keys
sections.body:
It's technically possible to generate a long-lived IAM user access key, paste it into an EC2 instance's environment variables or a config file, and have your application authenticate to AWS that way. It's also one of the most consistently flagged anti-patterns in AWS security guidance, for a very concrete reason: that access key is now a static secret sitting on disk (or in an environment) that never expires on its own, and every additional place a static secret sits is another place it can leak -- committed to a repo by accident, baked into an AMI, exposed via a misconfigured log line, or exfiltrated if the instance itself is ever compromised.

The alternative, and the standard practice, is an **IAM role attached to the instance via an instance profile**. Once attached, the EC2 Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) running locally on the instance automatically serves rotating, temporary credentials to any AWS SDK or CLI call made from that instance -- no access key is ever generated, stored, or transmitted by a human at all. The exact same pattern applies to a Lambda function's **execution role** and an ECS task's **task role**: the compute resource assumes a role, gets short-lived credentials scoped to whatever that role's policy allows, and those credentials are automatically refreshed and never need to be manually rotated. This eliminates an entire category of risk, not just reduces it -- there's no static secret sitting anywhere for an attacker (or an automated bot scraping public code repositories, which reliably finds and abuses exposed `AKIA...`-prefixed access keys within minutes of a push) to find in the first place.

sections.heading: Least Privilege, and the Trouble With Wildcards
sections.body:
The **principle of least privilege** says a policy should grant exactly the actions and resources a principal actually needs to do its job, and nothing more. It sounds obvious in the abstract and is routinely violated in practice, usually for a very understandable reason: while building something new, nobody wants to stop and figure out the exact minimal set of permissions required, so it's tempting to reach for `"Action": "s3:*"` or even `"Action": "*", "Resource": "*"` just to get unblocked -- with a mental note to 'tighten this up later' that, in a huge number of real codebases, simply never happens before the code ships to production.

The risk isn't hypothetical. A role with `s3:*` on `Resource: *` doesn't just let an application read the one bucket it actually needs -- it can also delete objects, delete entire buckets, and rewrite bucket policies on *every* S3 bucket in the account, including ones that have nothing to do with that application at all. If that role's credentials are ever misused (through a compromised dependency, an SSRF vulnerability, or any other route into the application), the blast radius is the entire account's S3 footprint, not just the one bucket the application was ever supposed to touch. The practical discipline that avoids this is to start narrow -- grant only the specific actions on the specific resources you know you need right now -- and expand deliberately as CloudTrail logs or IAM Access Advisor reveal genuinely needed permissions that were missed, rather than starting broad and hoping someone remembers to narrow it down before it matters. AWS's own IAM Access Analyzer tool exists specifically to help surface policies that are broader than their actual usage, precisely because this pattern is common enough to warrant automated tooling.

examples.title: A Least-Privilege S3 Policy vs. an Overly Broad One
examples.explanation: The narrow policy's `Resource` field is an ARN pattern that only matches objects inside `app-data-bucket` -- the `/*` suffix specifically means 'any object key within this bucket,' not the bucket itself. A principal with only this policy attached can read objects from that one bucket and can do literally nothing else in S3: it cannot delete anything, cannot list other buckets, cannot touch any other bucket in the account. The broad policy's `"s3:*"` on `"Resource": "*"` looks similar at a glance but grants every S3 action (`GetObject`, `PutObject`, `DeleteObject`, `DeleteBucket`, `PutBucketPolicy`, and dozens more) against every bucket that exists or will ever exist in the account. If this policy is attached to, say, a role used by a single reporting microservice, that microservice's credentials -- if ever leaked or misused -- become a master key to every S3 bucket AWS account-wide, including buckets that particular service was never even meant to know exist.

examples.title: An EC2 Instance Role's Trust Policy vs. Its Permissions Policy
examples.explanation: These are two genuinely different documents that are easy to conflate. The trust policy says which principal is allowed to call `sts:AssumeRole` on this role in the first place -- here, the EC2 service itself, which is what makes it possible to attach this role to an instance via an instance profile at all. Change the trust policy's `Principal` to `lambda.amazonaws.com` and the exact same role could instead be assumed by a Lambda function; change it to another AWS account's ARN and that account could assume it (a common cross-account access pattern). The permissions policy is entirely separate, and answers a different question: once something has successfully assumed this role, what is it actually allowed to do? Here, read and write access to one specific bucket's objects, nothing more. Mixing these two up -- for instance, assuming that broadening the trust policy somehow grants more permissions, or that the permissions policy controls who can use the role -- is one of the more common points of confusion for people newer to IAM.

examples.title: An Explicit Deny Overriding a Broad Allow
examples.explanation: Both policies are attached to the same role, and both are evaluated together for every request that role makes. Policy A's `s3:*` on `Resource: *` would, on its own, allow `DeleteBucket` along with everything else in S3. Policy B contains an explicit `Deny` that specifically matches `s3:DeleteBucket` on all resources. Because an explicit Deny always overrides any Allow, regardless of which policy it lives in or the order the policies were attached in, the net effect is: this role can do anything `s3:*` would normally allow, except delete a bucket, which is unconditionally blocked. This pattern -- a broad Allow paired with a narrow, deliberate Deny as a guardrail -- is a legitimate technique, but as the earlier explanation section notes, it's only as reliable as the Deny's own Action/Resource matching being exactly correct; a typo or overly narrow ARN in the Deny would silently leave the broad Allow fully exposed for whatever the Deny failed to actually catch.

misconceptions.description: IAM groups are a kind of principal, so you can write a policy's Principal field as a group, or a role can effectively 'be' a group.
misconceptions.clarification: A group is purely an administrative container for attaching policies to many users at once -- it is not itself a principal that can make API calls, be assumed, or be referenced in a `Principal` field of a trust or resource policy. Only users, roles, AWS services, and AWS accounts can act as principals. If you need a set of permissions that multiple different kinds of callers (say, both a human and an EC2 instance) should share, you attach the same policy document to each of their respective principals (a user and a role) individually -- groups only help with the specific case of many IAM users needing the same identity-based policy.

misconceptions.description: As long as a policy statement has Effect: Allow for a given action, that action is permitted.
misconceptions.clarification: An Allow only takes effect if there is no applicable explicit Deny anywhere else in scope -- across the principal's own identity-based policies, any relevant resource-based policy, any permissions boundary, and any AWS Organizations Service Control Policy. Because everything is denied by default and an explicit Deny always overrides any Allow no matter where it's defined, a seemingly sufficient Allow can still result in an access-denied outcome if any other applicable policy explicitly denies that same action or resource.

exercises.prompt: A developer wrote this policy intending to let an application role read objects only from the 'reports-bucket' S3 bucket. A security review found the role can actually read from every bucket in the account. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Look specifically at the Resource field -- what set of ARNs does the string it currently holds actually match?
An S3 object ARN has the shape arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name/key-name. What ARN pattern would match only objects inside reports-bucket, and nothing else?

Remember that the bucket's own ARN (arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket) and the objects inside it (arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*) are different resources -- GetObject acts on the object-level ARN, which needs the /* suffix.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original `"Resource": "*"` is a wildcard that matches every resource ARN in existence, across every AWS service and every bucket in the account -- not just objects in one bucket. The fix scopes the Resource field to `arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket/*`, an ARN pattern that only matches object keys within the reports-bucket bucket specifically. It's worth noting a companion mistake this same misunderstanding often produces: if the role also needed to call `s3:ListBucket` (to enumerate what's in the bucket, as opposed to reading a specific known object), that action applies to the bucket's own ARN without the `/*` suffix, since listing is an operation on the bucket resource itself, not on any individual object -- a second, separate statement with `"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::reports-bucket"` would be needed for that, and it's a common follow-up bug to forget.

exercises.prompt: Write a least-privilege identity-based IAM policy (JSON) that allows a role to both read and write objects -- but never delete them -- and only within the 'uploads/' prefix of a bucket named 'user-uploads-bucket'. The role should not be able to do anything else.
hints: Which two S3 action names correspond to reading and writing an object? Since delete should never be permitted, does the policy need a Deny for it, or can it simply omit that action from the Allow entirely?
The Resource ARN needs to express 'any object key under the uploads/ prefix inside user-uploads-bucket' -- think about where the wildcard needs to go relative to the prefix.
Double-check scope: the exercise only asks for object-level get/put access under a prefix, not bucket-level actions like ListBucket -- don't grant permissions beyond what was actually asked for.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The `Action` array lists only `s3:GetObject` and `s3:PutObject` -- omitting `s3:DeleteObject` entirely satisfies 'never delete' more robustly than granting it and then trying to cancel it out with a separate Deny statement, since simply never allowing an action in the first place can't be defeated by a mismatched or missing Deny elsewhere. The `Resource` ARN, `arn:aws:s3:::user-uploads-bucket/uploads/*`, scopes access to only object keys that begin with the `uploads/` prefix inside that one bucket -- an object like `user-uploads-bucket/exports/report.csv` would not match this pattern at all. The policy deliberately does not include `s3:ListBucket`, since that's a bucket-level action (it would need the bare bucket ARN, `arn:aws:s3:::user-uploads-bucket`, as its Resource, not the object-level ARN used here) and the exercise only asked for get/put access to objects under a prefix -- least privilege means resisting the temptation to add 'while I'm at it' permissions that weren't actually requested.

assessments.prompt: An engineer attaches two policies to the same IAM role: Policy A allows `s3:*` on `Resource: *`. Policy B explicitly denies `s3:DeleteObject` on `Resource: *`. What can the role actually do?
options: Everything s3:* allows, including DeleteObject, because Policy A was attached first.
Nothing at all, because the two conflicting policies cancel each other out entirely.
Everything s3:* allows except DeleteObject, because an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow regardless of attachment order.
Only DeleteObject is blocked temporarily until an administrator manually resolves the conflict between the two policies.
assessments.explanation: IAM policy evaluation always applies the rule that an explicit Deny overrides any Allow for the same action and resource, regardless of which policy document it's written in or the order policies were attached -- there's no such concept as attachment order mattering (option A), no concept of policies 'canceling out' into total denial (option B, which would incorrectly also block every other s3 action the role needs), and no manual resolution step required at evaluation time (option D -- the Deny simply always wins immediately, automatically, on every request). The correct outcome is that the role retains every permission s3:* grants except specifically DeleteObject, which the explicit Deny blocks unconditionally.

assessments.prompt: An IAM role's trust policy currently has `{ "Principal": { "Service": "ec2.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": "sts:AssumeRole" }`. A team now wants a Lambda function, instead of an EC2 instance, to be able to assume this same role and use its existing permissions policy unchanged. What must they change?
options: Nothing -- any AWS service can assume any role automatically, regardless of what its trust policy's Principal says.
The role's permissions policy, by adding `lambda:InvokeFunction` to its Action list.

The role's trust policy, updating its Principal to include `lambda.amazonaws.com`, since the trust policy -- not the permissions policy -- controls which service or principal is allowed to call sts:AssumeRole on the role.
Nothing can be changed -- a role's trust policy is permanently fixed to whichever service it was originally created for.
assessments.explanation: The trust policy and the permissions policy answer two different questions: the trust policy says who is allowed to assume the role in the first place, and the permissions policy says what the role can do once assumed. Since the permissions policy doesn't need to change at all (the desired permissions are already correct), the only thing that needs updating is the trust policy's Principal, from the EC2 service to the Lambda service -- exactly the kind of substitution the underlying example calls out explicitly. Option A is wrong because AssumeRole is gated by the trust policy, not granted universally; option B confuses the permissions policy with the trust policy; option D is wrong because trust policies are ordinary, editable IAM documents, not permanently fixed at creation.

assessments.prompt: A team wants an IAM user (used by a developer) and an IAM role (assumed by an EC2 instance) to share an identical set of permissions, and considers creating an IAM group that both the user and the role could join. What is the problem with this plan?
options: Nothing -- IAM groups can contain both users and roles, so adding both to the same group is a standard way to share permissions.

A group is not itself a principal and cannot be assumed or referenced as a Principal, and a role cannot be placed into a group at all -- the correct approach is to attach the same policy document directly to both the user and the role.
The plan works, but only for roles attached to EC2 instances specifically, not Lambda functions.
Groups can only be used with resource-based policies, not identity-based policies, so this plan would need a bucket policy instead.
assessments.explanation: A group is purely an administrative container for attaching a policy to many IAM users at once -- it is not a principal, cannot be assumed via sts:AssumeRole, cannot appear in a Principal field, and critically, roles cannot be added to groups at all (only users can be group members). Achieving identical permissions across a user and a role that aren't both users requires attaching the same policy document to each of them individually, exactly as the misconception in this concept's material describes. Option C invents a distinction between EC2 and Lambda roles that doesn't exist for this purpose, and option D misdescribes what groups can be used with -- they only ever affect identity-based policy attachment for users, never resource-based policies.

assessments.prompt: A new engineer on your team wants to give a Lambda function access to AWS resources by generating an IAM user access key and storing it as an environment variable in the function's configuration. Explain why this is generally the wrong approach and what to do instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: The core problem is that an IAM user's access key is a static, long-lived secret that doesn't expire on its own -- once it exists, it's a permanent credential sitting somewhere (here, in the Lambda function's environment configuration) that has to be manually rotated and manually revoked if it's ever compromised, and every additional place a static secret is stored is another opportunity for it to leak, whether through a misconfigured log, an overly permissive IAM policy on who can read the function's configuration, or simple human error like it being copied into a script that later gets committed somewhere it shouldn't be. The correct approach is to give the Lambda function an execution role instead: attach an IAM role to the function, write a permissions policy on that role scoped to exactly what the function needs (following least privilege, not a broad grant), and let Lambda's own infrastructure handle assuming that role and injecting short-lived, automatically-rotating temporary credentials into the function's runtime environment via AWS's Security Token Service. The AWS SDK, when used inside a Lambda function, automatically discovers and uses these temporary credentials with no code changes required -- there's no access key to generate, store, or ever manually rotate, and if the function's underlying credentials were somehow exposed, they'd already be expiring on a short window rather than remaining valid indefinitely like a static user access key would. This is the same underlying pattern used for EC2 instance roles and ECS task roles: compute resources that need AWS access should assume a role, not carry a long-lived user's static credentials.

concepts.title: EC2 and Instance Types
concepts.description: EC2 rents virtual machines by the type and by the second, and picking the right instance family and size is about matching your workload's actual bottleneck -- CPU, memory, network, or burst pattern -- to what you pay for, not simply picking bigger.
learningObjectives: Explain what EC2 actually provides -- a virtualized, isolated slice of physical hardware -- and how that differs from provisioning an on-premises server.
Decode an instance type name (e.g. m6g.xlarge, c6i.2xlarge) into its family, generation, capability flags, and size.
Match an instance family to a workload profile (compute-bound, memory-bound, burstable, network-intensive).
Explain burstable (t-family) CPU credits and why a sustained high-CPU workload on a t-family instance is a common performance and cost trap.
Distinguish On-Demand, Reserved/Savings Plans, and Spot pricing models and identify which is appropriate for a given workload.

sections.heading: What EC2 Actually Gives You
sections.body:
EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) provides virtual machines running on top of AWS's own hypervisor (the Nitro System, on current-generation instances): when you launch an instance, you're allocated an isolated slice of a physical host's CPU cores, memory, and network bandwidth, kept strictly separated from every other customer's instances that might be running on the same underlying hardware. The practical difference from provisioning an on-premises server is less about the hardware itself and more about the economics and elasticity around it: there's no procurement lead time (an instance is running within roughly a minute of the API call that launches it), you pay per second or per hour only while it's running, and when you're done, you terminate it and simply stop paying -- there's no depreciating asset sitting in a rack afterward.

A detail worth flagging early because it surprises people coming from a traditional server background: an EC2 instance's root volume is, by default, backed by EBS (Elastic Block Store) -- a separate, network-attached block storage service, not physically part of the same host as the compute. This is exactly what allows an instance to be stopped and its root volume detached and reattached to a different underlying host on restart, and it's a different service from the S3 object storage covered in a later concept -- EBS behaves like an attached disk with a filesystem on it; S3 does not.

sections.heading: Decoding an Instance Type Name
sections.body:
An instance type name like `m6g.xlarge` or `c6i.2xlarge` packs several pieces of information into a short string, and being able to read it fluently is genuinely useful day to day. The leading letter is the **family**, which signals the intended workload profile: `m` (general purpose, a balanced ratio of CPU to memory), `c` (compute optimized, more CPU per dollar, less memory), `r` (memory optimized, more RAM per dollar, less relative CPU), `t` (burstable general purpose, covered in detail below), and `g`/`p` (GPU-accelerated, for ML training/inference or graphics workloads). The number after the family letter is the **generation** -- `6` is newer than `5` at the same family, generally meaning better price-performance from newer underlying hardware, and it's usually worth using the newest generation available unless something specific (like software certified only against an older generation) argues otherwise. Extra lowercase letters after the generation number are **capability flags**: `g` here specifically means the instance uses AWS's own Graviton (ARM-based) processor rather than an x86 chip -- Graviton instances are frequently both cheaper and more power-efficient for workloads that don't depend on x86-specific binaries, but they do require your software to run on ARM (either natively, or via multi-architecture container images). Finally, the part after the dot is the **size** (`nano`, `micro`, `small`, `medium`, `large`, `xlarge`, `2xlarge`, ...), where each step up roughly doubles vCPU count and memory versus the previous size within the same family.

The reason this matters beyond trivia: family choice should follow your actual bottleneck, not a habit or a guess. A batch video-transcoding job that pegs every CPU core is compute-bound and belongs on a `c`-family instance. An in-memory cache or a database that's constantly RAM-constrained but not CPU-constrained belongs on an `r`-family instance -- moving it to a bigger `c`-family instance would add CPU it doesn't need while barely improving the memory ceiling that's actually the constraint. A web server with a low average load but occasional short bursts might be a legitimate fit for the cheaper `t`-family, with the specific caveat covered next.

sections.heading: Burstable Instances and CPU Credits: The t-family Gotcha
sections.body:
`t`-family instances (`t3`, `t3a`, `t4g`, and so on) are priced assuming that most workloads spend most of their time well below full CPU utilization, with only occasional short spikes above it -- a very common real-world traffic pattern, and one AWS prices these instances to reward. Each `t`-family instance has a **baseline performance** level and continuously earns **CPU credits** while running below that baseline; it spends credits to burst above baseline when demand spikes. As long as bursts are genuinely occasional and brief, the accumulated credit balance comfortably absorbs them and you get burst-capable performance at a fraction of the cost of a fixed-performance instance sized for peak load.

The trap appears when load isn't actually occasional -- if a workload runs sustained high CPU for hours rather than short bursts, it burns through its accumulated credit balance faster than it's replenished, and once the balance hits zero, behavior depends on the account's configured **credit mode**: in the default 'standard' mode, the instance's CPU performance is throttled down hard, right back to the (much lower) baseline level, often producing a confusing performance cliff that looks like the instance 'suddenly got slow' with no code change to explain it; in 'unlimited' mode, the instance keeps performing above baseline but starts incurring additional charges for the extra CPU usage, which can produce an unexpected bill spike instead of a performance cliff. Either way, the underlying lesson is the same: `t`-family instances are a genuinely good fit for spiky-but-mostly-idle workloads, and a genuinely bad fit for anything with a sustained high baseline load -- that workload should be sized onto a fixed-performance family (`m`, `c`, or `r`, depending on the actual bottleneck) instead.

sections.heading: Pricing Models: On-Demand, Reserved/Savings Plans, and Spot
sections.body: The same instance type can be purchased under different commitment models, and the right choice depends entirely on how predictable and how interruption-tolerant the workload is. **On-Demand** pricing has no commitment at all -- you pay a per-second or per-hour rate only while the instance runs, it's the most expensive rate per hour among the three, and it's the right default for anything unpredictable, short-lived, or still being sized (you're not locking in a wrong guess). **Reserved Instances** and their more flexible modern successor, **Savings Plans**, involve committing to a 1-year or 3-year term (with various payment options) in exchange for a substantial discount -- often up to roughly 70% off On-Demand pricing for the longest commitments. These make sense for a workload you already know will run continuously, essentially 24/7, for the length of the commitment -- a baseline production fleet is the classic case, not a workload you're still validating. **Spot Instances** let you bid for AWS's genuinely spare compute capacity at a very steep discount, often 70-90% off On-Demand -- in exchange for AWS being able to reclaim that capacity back, with as little as a two-minute warning, whenever it's needed elsewhere. Spot is an excellent fit for workloads that are stateless, checkpointable, or cheaply retryable -- batch data processing, CI/CD runners, rendering jobs, or a horizontally-scaled stateless web fleet that can absorb losing any individual instance without user-visible impact -- and a genuinely bad fit for anything stateful that can't tolerate sudden, largely unannounced termination, like a single-instance database with no replication.

sections.heading: AMIs: The Template an Instance Launches From
sections.body:
Every EC2 instance launches from an **AMI** (Amazon Machine Image) -- a template that bundles a root volume snapshot along with launch metadata (like which architecture and virtualization type it supports). AWS publishes maintained AMIs for common operating systems (Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, Windows Server), the AWS Marketplace offers third-party vendor AMIs, and you can also bake your own **custom AMI**: install your application and its dependencies onto a running instance exactly the way you want it, then create an AMI from that instance's current state.

The practical payoff of a custom AMI shows up once you have more than a handful of instances, and especially once autoscaling enters the picture (the subject of a later concept in this subject): if new instances launch from a generic base AMI and then run a lengthy bootstrap script to install everything on every boot, scaling out under sudden load is slow, and any transient failure partway through that bootstrap script produces an inconsistent, half-configured instance. Baking a custom AMI with everything pre-installed means a newly launched instance is fully ready essentially the moment it boots, with launch time and configuration reliability that a from-scratch bootstrap script simply can't match at scale -- this is precisely why 'golden AMI' pipelines (rebuild and republish an AMI on every application release) are a standard practice in mature AWS deployments.

examples.title: Decoding Three Instance Type Names Against Their Likely Workloads
examples.code:
m6g.xlarge   -> m = general purpose, 6 = 6th gen, g = Graviton (ARM), xlarge size
             -> balanced CPU/memory; good default for a typical web/app server

c6i.2xlarge  -> c = compute optimized, 6 = 6th gen, i = Intel, 2xlarge size
             -> CPU-heavy ratio; good for video encoding, batch computation, CI build fleets

r5.large     -> r = memory optimized, 5 = 5th gen, (no extra flag = x86, non-Graviton), large size
             -> high RAM-to-CPU ratio; good for in-memory caches, large in-memory databases
examples.explanation: None of these three names are arbitrary -- each maps directly onto a workload decision. `m6g.xlarge` is the safe, balanced default when you don't yet know your actual bottleneck (a new service in early development, for instance), and the `g` flag means it also happens to be one of the cheaper-per-vCPU options available, provided your software runs on ARM. `c6i.2xlarge` trades away relative memory for more CPU per dollar, which only pays off if the workload is genuinely CPU-bound -- putting a memory-bound workload here wastes money on CPU capacity that never gets used while the actual memory constraint barely improves. `r5.large` is the mirror image: more memory per dollar, less relative CPU, ideal for something like an in-memory cache where CPU usage is minimal but the size of the dataset that fits in RAM directly determines performance. Choosing between these should be driven by which resource (CPU or memory) is actually saturated according to CloudWatch metrics under real load -- not by guessing or defaulting to whichever size 'sounds about right.'

examples.title: Launching an Instance Tied to a Specific AZ and IAM Role
examples.code:
aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0abcdef1234567890 \
  --instance-type m6g.large \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=app-server-role \
  --subnet-id subnet-0f1e2d3c \
  --security-group-ids sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
  --count 1
examples.explanation: This single command pulls together several earlier ideas. `--image-id` specifies the AMI this instance boots from -- if it's a custom AMI, the instance comes up with the application already installed, no bootstrap script required. `--instance-type m6g.large` picks a balanced, Graviton-based family and size appropriate for a general-purpose app server. `--subnet-id subnet-0f1e2d3c` implicitly pins this instance to whichever single Availability Zone that subnet belongs to -- launching a second instance for redundancy would require a *different* subnet ID from a different AZ, exactly as covered in the Regions/AZs concept. `--iam-instance-profile Name=app-server-role` attaches an IAM role rather than embedding any access key -- the instance's SDK calls will authenticate using temporary credentials served automatically by the instance metadata service, exactly as covered in the IAM fundamentals concept. Each flag here is a direct, concrete application of a concept from earlier in this module, not an isolated new idea.

examples.title: The Burstable-Instance Trap: Watching CPU Credits Run Out
examples.code:
time      CPUUtilization   CPUCreditBalance   note
09:00     15%               144                idle-ish, earning credits
09:15     20%               150                still earning
09:30     85%               140                burst begins, spending credits
10:00     85%                60                sustained burst, balance dropping fast
10:30     85%                 0                balance exhausted
10:31     22%                 2                THROTTLED to baseline -- utilization capped, NOT by demand
examples.explanation: The CPUUtilization column alone would look like a normal, if elevated, load pattern -- nothing here screams 'error.' The CPUCreditBalance column tells the real story: this instance began accumulating credits while idling below baseline, then at 09:30 something (a traffic spike, a batch job, anything sustained) pushed it well above baseline, and it started spending credits faster than it was earning them. By 10:30 the balance hits zero, and at 10:31 CPUUtilization abruptly drops to 22% -- not because demand dropped, but because the instance has been throttled back down to its baseline performance level in standard credit mode, and simply can no longer deliver more CPU than that regardless of how much load is actually waiting. From the application's point of view, this looks exactly like an unexplained performance cliff; from the infrastructure's point of view, it's an entirely predictable consequence of running a sustained workload on a burstable instance family that was priced and designed for occasional, short bursts, not sustained load.

misconceptions.description: If you're not sure what instance type you need, picking a bigger and more expensive one is always the safe choice.
misconceptions.clarification: 'Bigger' only helps if it adds capacity in the dimension that's actually bottlenecked. Moving a CPU-bound encoding job onto a larger memory-optimized instance adds RAM it was never short on while leaving the real CPU constraint barely touched -- money spent with no meaningful performance gain. Right-sizing means looking at actual CloudWatch metrics (CPU, memory via the CloudWatch agent, network, disk) to identify which resource is genuinely saturated, then choosing a family that targets that specific resource, rather than defaulting to 'bigger' as a substitute for actually diagnosing the bottleneck.

misconceptions.description: Spot Instances are just a cheaper version of On-Demand with no meaningful downside besides the discount.
misconceptions.clarification: Spot Instances can be reclaimed by AWS with as little as a two-minute warning whenever AWS needs that capacity back for other customers -- this is a fundamentally different reliability contract from On-Demand, not merely a pricing difference. Spot is an excellent fit specifically for workloads that are stateless, checkpointable, or cheaply retryable (batch jobs, CI runners, horizontally-scaled stateless fleets), and a poor fit for anything stateful or latency-sensitive that can't gracefully absorb sudden, largely unannounced termination.

exercises.prompt: A t3.micro instance runs sustained CPU load at 80% utilization for several hours straight, well above its baseline. Given what you know about CPU credits, predict what happens to its performance over that period, and why.
exercises.code:
credit_mode: standard
baseline_performance_pct: 20
starting_credit_balance: 144
observed_utilization: 80%  (sustained for hours)
hints: Is this instance earning credits or spending them while running at 80%, given that its baseline is only 20%?
A finite starting balance being spent faster than it's replenished will eventually reach zero -- what does 'standard' credit mode do at that point?
Think about what happens to CPUUtilization itself, not just the credit balance, once the balance hits zero and standard mode kicks in its behavior.
exercises.expectedAnswer: The instance spends credits continuously (since 80% is well above the 20% baseline), draining the starting balance of 144 over some number of hours until it hits zero. At that point, standard credit mode throttles the instance's CPU performance down to its 20% baseline -- CPUUtilization will drop sharply (not because load decreased, but because the instance can no longer deliver more), producing a sudden, confusing performance degradation with no corresponding drop in actual demand.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Running at 80% against a 20% baseline means the instance is spending CPU credits on every sample throughout the whole period, with no offsetting accumulation, so the 144-credit starting balance depletes steadily and predictably. Once it reaches zero, standard credit mode enforces the baseline as a hard ceiling -- the instance is throttled to roughly 20% utilization regardless of how much demand is actually waiting to be served, which from a monitoring dashboard looks like utilization suddenly falling even though nothing about the incoming load changed. This is exactly the scenario that argues for either switching this instance to unlimited credit mode (accepting extra charges to sustain the burst) or, if the load is genuinely sustained rather than occasional, moving it off the t-family entirely onto a fixed-performance family sized for that actual baseline.

exercises.prompt: A team runs an in-memory caching layer (similar to Redis) on a c5.xlarge instance. They keep seeing frequent evictions and out-of-memory errors even though CPUUtilization stays consistently low. Diagnose the instance-type bug and propose a fix.
exercises.code:
instance_type: c5.xlarge     # compute optimized, 4 vCPU / 8 GiB RAM
workload: in-memory-cache
observed_cpu_utilization: 12%
observed_symptom: frequent evictions, occasional OOM errors
hints: Low CPU utilization alongside memory pressure is a strong signal about which resource is actually the bottleneck here.
The c-family is compute optimized specifically because it trades away relative memory for more CPU -- is that ratio a good match for a workload whose entire job is holding data in RAM?
Look for a family explicitly optimized for a high memory-to-CPU ratio, at a comparable size, rather than simply moving to a bigger instance within the same family.
exercises.solutionCode:
instance_type: r5.xlarge      # memory optimized, 4 vCPU / 32 GiB RAM
workload: in-memory-cache
# same vCPU count as before, ~4x the RAM -- targets the actual bottleneck directly
exercises.solutionExplanation: 12% CPU utilization alongside frequent evictions and OOM errors is a textbook memory bottleneck, not a compute one -- the instance is running out of RAM to hold the cache's working set long before it comes anywhere close to running out of CPU. The original c5.xlarge is compute optimized, meaning its 8 GiB of RAM is deliberately modest relative to its CPU allocation, which is exactly backwards for a workload whose entire purpose is holding as much data in memory as possible. Switching to r5.xlarge keeps the same vCPU count (so nothing about compute capacity changes) but roughly quadruples available RAM to 32 GiB, directly targeting the resource that was actually constrained. Simply moving to a bigger c-family instance (e.g. c5.2xlarge) would have thrown more money at more CPU the workload never needed, while only modestly improving the memory ceiling that was the real problem.

assessments.prompt: A nightly batch job compresses large video files and finishes faster with more CPU cores available, but its memory usage stays low and predictable throughout. Which instance family is the most appropriate choice?
options: An r-family (memory optimized) instance, to comfortably hold each file in memory during processing.
A t-family (burstable) instance, since the job only runs briefly once per night.
A c-family (compute optimized) instance, to maximize CPU throughput per dollar for this CPU-bound workload.
The cheapest available instance type regardless of family, since batch jobs are not latency-sensitive.
assessments.explanation: The workload is explicitly described as CPU-bound (finishes faster with more cores) with low, predictable memory usage -- that's precisely the profile a compute-optimized c-family instance targets, maximizing CPU per dollar rather than paying for memory headroom the job doesn't use (which rules out option A). Option B is a trap: 'runs briefly once per night' sounds like it matches burstable instances' occasional-use pricing model, but a nightly batch job sustaining high CPU for its entire duration is exactly the sustained-load pattern that exhausts t-family CPU credits and triggers throttling -- brief-but-sustained-at-full-intensity is not the same as brief-but-idle-most-of-the-time. Option D ignores the workload profile entirely; the cheapest instance type is only a good choice if it also happens to match the actual bottleneck, which for a CPU-bound job is what the c-family is specifically built for.

assessments.prompt: A team is considering switching their fleet from c6i.2xlarge to c6g.2xlarge to reduce cost. What must be true for this migration to work correctly?
options: Nothing needs to change -- the letters after the generation number are purely cosmetic and never affect compatibility.
Their application (or its container images) must support the ARM architecture, since the 'g' flag indicates AWS's Graviton (ARM-based) processor, while the 'i' flag indicates an Intel x86 chip.
They must move up to a larger size, such as 4xlarge, to compensate for a slower clock speed on Graviton hardware.
Graviton instances only run Windows Server, so this migration only matters if the fleet currently runs Windows.
assessments.explanation: The lowercase letters after the generation number are capability flags, not decoration -- 'g' specifically means the instance runs on AWS's Graviton (ARM) processor rather than an x86 chip like the 'i' (Intel) variant. Since ARM and x86 are different instruction set architectures, software (or container images) built only for x86 will not run unmodified on Graviton; the migration is only safe once the application is confirmed to run on ARM, whether natively or via multi-architecture images. Option A misreads capability flags as meaningless, option C invents a clock-speed compensation requirement that isn't how instance sizing works, and option D fabricates an OS restriction that doesn't exist -- Graviton instances run Linux (and increasingly Windows) just as x86 instances do, the real constraint is architecture compatibility, not OS.

assessments.prompt: Two teams each run a t3.medium instance that occasionally exceeds its baseline CPU performance. Team A's instance uses 'standard' credit mode; Team B's uses 'unlimited' credit mode. Both instances exhaust their CPU credit balance during a sustained traffic spike. What happens to each?
options: Both instances are throttled identically back to baseline performance, since credit mode only changes how fast credits are earned, not what happens when they run out.

Team A's instance is throttled down to its baseline performance level; Team B's instance keeps performing above baseline but starts incurring additional charges for the extra CPU usage beyond what its credits covered.
Team A's instance is automatically terminated when its credit balance reaches zero; Team B's instance is throttled instead.
Both instances continue performing above baseline indefinitely at no extra charge, because credit balances regenerate instantly once they hit zero.
assessments.explanation: Credit mode specifically governs what happens once the credit balance is exhausted, not just how credits accumulate. In standard mode, once credits run out, CPU performance is hard-throttled back down to the baseline level -- Team A's instance visibly slows down regardless of how much demand remains. In unlimited mode, the instance is allowed to keep bursting above baseline even with a zero or negative credit balance, but AWS bills for that additional usage instead of throttling it -- Team B's instance keeps performing but the bill reflects the overage. Option A collapses this real distinction, option C invents an automatic-termination behavior that doesn't happen from credit exhaustion alone, and option D ignores that credits are a finite, gradually-replenished resource, not something that resets instantly.

assessments.prompt: Explain how you would decide between On-Demand, Reserved Instances/Savings Plans, and Spot Instances for three different workloads: a steady-state production API fleet that runs 24/7 year-round, a nightly data-processing batch job that can be retried if interrupted, and a brand-new service whose traffic pattern isn't well understood yet.
assessments.modelAnswer: The right pricing model follows directly from how predictable and how interruption-tolerant each workload actually is, not from which one is simply cheapest in isolation. The steady-state production API fleet running continuously year-round is exactly the case Reserved Instances or Savings Plans are built for: since you already know with high confidence that this capacity will be running essentially all the time for at least a year, committing to that term captures a substantial discount -- often up to around 70% off On-Demand -- for capacity you were going to pay for anyway, with no meaningful downside since there's no uncertainty being locked in. The nightly batch job is the classic Spot Instance candidate: it's explicitly described as retryable, meaning an interruption (which Spot can impose with as little as two minutes' notice when AWS reclaims the capacity) simply means the job retries rather than causing a real incident, so it's worth accepting that risk in exchange for the very steep Spot discount, often 70-90% off On-Demand, especially for a workload that isn't user-facing or time-critical to the minute. The brand-new service with an unknown traffic pattern should run On-Demand, at least initially: committing to a 1- or 3-year Reserved Instance term before you know the real steady-state capacity you'll need risks locking in the wrong instance count or type, and On-Demand's lack of commitment is exactly what lets you observe real usage and right-size before making any longer-term financial commitment -- the discount from Reserved capacity isn't worth the risk of committing to a guess that turns out wrong. In practice, mature AWS accounts typically end up running a blend: a Reserved/Savings-Plan-covered baseline sized to known steady-state load, On-Demand or Spot capacity layered on top to absorb variable or uncertain demand, adjusted over time as usage patterns become clearer.

concepts.title: S3 and Object Storage Semantics
concepts.description: S3 stores objects, not files in a directory tree -- understanding that distinction, alongside its durability and consistency guarantees and its storage classes, is what lets you design around S3 correctly instead of fighting its actual model.
learningObjectives: Explain why S3 is an object store rather than a filesystem, and what that implies for operations like renaming or listing at scale.
Explain S3's durability design and why it is a distinct guarantee from availability.
Explain S3's strong read-after-write consistency model and why older material describes a different, weaker guarantee.
Choose an appropriate storage class for a given access pattern and cost/latency requirement, and describe how a lifecycle policy automates transitions between classes.
Distinguish IAM policies, bucket policies, and Block Public Access as different layers of S3 access control, and explain what each one governs.

sections.heading: Objects, Not Files: What S3 Actually Stores
sections.body:
An S3 **object** is the combination of the data itself (arbitrary bytes, up to 5TB per object), a set of metadata, and a unique **key** -- a string that identifies that object within a **bucket**.
