That's the entire model: a flat namespace of keys mapped to objects inside a bucket, with no real directory tree underneath, even though the AWS console displays something that looks exactly like nested folders. The console's 'folders' are a display convenience built entirely on the fact that keys are allowed to contain `/` characters -- a key like `logs/2026/01/app.log` is really just one string with slashes in it, and the console groups keys by shared prefixes to render something that *looks* hierarchical. There's no actual folder object being created, moved, or renamed underneath.

This has a very concrete practical consequence: there is no atomic 'rename' operation on an object, and there is definitely no atomic rename on a 'folder.' Renaming an object is implemented as copy-to-new-key followed by delete-old-key -- two separate API calls, not one. Renaming what looks like a folder containing a million objects that share a prefix means issuing that copy-then-delete sequence *individually*, for every single one of those million objects, since there is no single operation that renames a prefix. This is precisely why bulk 'moving' large numbers of objects in S3 can be slow and can rack up a real request-count cost that catches people off guard the first time they try it on a genuinely large object count -- it isn't one operation pretending to be many, it actually is many operations.

sections.heading: Durability vs. Availability: 11 Nines Doesn't Mean What People Assume
sections.body:
S3 Standard advertises 99.999999999% durability -- eleven nines -- and it's worth being precise about what that number is actually claiming, because it's frequently misread. Durability is a statement about **data loss**: S3 redundantly stores each object's underlying data across multiple devices, in multiple Availability Zones within the Region, specifically so that a hardware failure -- a failed disk, a failed rack, even a failed AZ -- essentially never results in an object's bytes being permanently lost. Over a large enough number of objects and a long enough time horizon, that eleven-nines figure describes just how astronomically unlikely permanent data loss is.

Availability is a separate axis entirely: it's about whether the *service* is reachable and successfully responding to requests at any given moment, and S3 Standard's published availability target is considerably lower, around 99.99%. That gap matters in practice -- there can be a brief moment where a particular GET request fails or times out (an availability blip, however rare) while the underlying object data was never actually at risk of being lost (durability fully intact). Conflating the two leads to a specific, avoidable mistake: assuming that because durability is essentially bulletproof, retry logic around S3 calls is unnecessary. It isn't -- code that calls S3 should still handle occasional request failures gracefully (with retries and backoff), because that's governed by the availability guarantee, not the durability one.

sections.heading: Consistency: Strong Read-After-Write (and a Bit of History Worth Knowing)
sections.body:
As of a change AWS shipped in December 2020, S3 provides **strong read-after-write consistency** for all operations: a `GET` issued immediately after a successful `PUT` will always return the object's latest version, and a list operation always reflects every write that completed before the list request was made -- no waiting, no possibility of reading stale or missing data. This sounds like an unremarkable baseline expectation today, but it's genuinely worth knowing the history, because a large amount of still-circulating material -- older blog posts, older StackOverflow answers, and defensive application code written to work around the *old* behavior -- assumes the earlier, weaker model, where overwrite `PUT`s and `DELETE`s in some cases only became eventually consistent, meaning a read immediately after a write could, for a brief window, return stale or missing data.

That older model caused real, hard-to-reproduce application bugs: write an object, immediately read it back to confirm, and occasionally get a miss or an old version, with no error raised anywhere to explain why. You'll still encounter code bases with retry loops or artificial delays inserted specifically to work around that old behavior; on modern S3, those workarounds are no longer necessary for consistency reasons (retry logic for plain request failures, per the availability discussion above, is still worth keeping) -- it's useful to recognize this pattern when you see it in an older codebase, rather than assuming it must still be protecting against something real.

sections.heading: Storage Classes: Trading Retrieval Speed and Cost for Storage Cost
sections.body:
S3 offers multiple storage classes that trade cheaper per-GB storage cost against slower retrieval, a per-retrieval fee, or reduced redundancy -- and the right choice is entirely about matching the class to the object's actual access pattern, not simply picking the cheapest one available. **S3 Standard** is priced for frequently accessed data with no retrieval fee and millisecond access. **Standard-IA** ('infrequent access') and **One Zone-IA** offer cheaper per-GB storage in exchange for a per-GB retrieval fee -- appropriate for data you access rarely but still need available instantly when you do (One Zone-IA additionally stores data in only a single AZ rather than multiple, trading some durability/availability margin for an even lower price, which is a reasonable trade only for data you could regenerate or that has a copy elsewhere). The **Glacier** family (Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, and Deep Archive) is built for archival data accessed rarely if ever, with per-GB storage costs that are dramatically lower still, in exchange for retrieval times ranging from milliseconds (Instant) to minutes or hours (Flexible) to potentially many hours (Deep Archive, the cheapest tier of all). **Intelligent-Tiering** automatically monitors access patterns per object and moves objects between frequent- and infrequent-access tiers on your behalf, which is a sensible default when you genuinely don't know, or can't predict, how a given dataset will actually be accessed over time.

Manually managing which objects sit in which class doesn't scale -- the standard practice is a **lifecycle policy**, a rule attached to the bucket (optionally scoped to a key prefix) that automatically transitions objects between classes based on age, and can also expire (permanently delete) objects after a set number of days. A very common real pattern: application logs written to S3 Standard while they're recent and might need to be queried, automatically transitioned to Standard-IA after 30 days once query frequency has dropped off, then to Glacier after 90 days for cheap long-term retention, then expired entirely after a year once even compliance-driven retention requirements are satisfied -- all without anyone manually moving a single object.

sections.heading: Controlling Access: IAM Policies, Bucket Policies, and Block Public Access
sections.body:
S3 access control involves several distinct layers that are worth being able to name separately, because a real access problem -- or a real accidental-exposure incident -- can originate from any one of them. **IAM identity-based policies**, attached to a user or role, describe what that principal is generally allowed to do in S3 (covered in depth in the IAM fundamentals concept). **Bucket policies** are resource-based policies attached directly to the bucket itself, and they're distinct in an important way: they can grant access to principals in *other* AWS accounts, or to the public at large, which is not something an identity-based policy attached to your own users can do on its own. This is also exactly where the overwhelming majority of 'a bucket became publicly accessible' incidents originate -- someone writes a bucket policy with an overly broad `Principal` (often `"*"`) intending to grant access to one specific consumer, and it ends up granting it to everyone. Legacy object and bucket **ACLs** are an older, largely superseded access-control mechanism that AWS now actively recommends disabling on new buckets in favor of policies, which are more expressive and easier to reason about.

**Block Public Access** is a separate safety mechanism layered on top of all of this, configurable at the account level or the individual bucket level: when enabled, it actively prevents public access from taking effect, even if a bucket policy or an ACL would otherwise grant it. AWS made this setting default-on for all newly created buckets specifically because years of exactly the bucket-policy-typo incident described above led to enough real, damaging data leaks that a mistake-resistant default became the right call -- you now have to make a deliberate decision to disable Block Public Access before a public-granting bucket policy can actually take effect, which adds a real speed bump in front of what used to be an easy, easy-to-miss mistake.

examples.title: Why 'Renaming a Folder' Is Actually Copying Every Object
examples.code:
aws s3 mv s3://reports-bucket/2025-exports/ s3://reports-bucket/archive/2025-exports/ --recursive

# Under the hood, for every single object matching the old prefix, the CLI issues:
#   1. a CopyObject call to the new key
#   2. a DeleteObject call on the old key
# There is no single S3 API call that renames a prefix as one atomic operation.
examples.explanation: This command looks like it should be a fast, cheap metadata-only rename -- and for a handful of objects, it's fast enough that the underlying mechanics don't matter. But because S3 has no real directory structure, 'the folder' `2025-exports/` isn't a thing that can be renamed; it's just a shared prefix across however many individual object keys happen to match it. The AWS CLI's `--recursive mv` handles this correctly by looping over every matching key and issuing a copy followed by a delete for each one -- which means if that prefix contains, say, two million objects, this single command line is actually about four million individual API calls under the hood, each contributing to request-based cost and each taking real time. Knowing this changes how you'd design around a genuinely large-scale reorganization -- for instance, by choosing key naming schemes upfront that you won't need to bulk-rename later, rather than assuming a rename will be as cheap as it would be on a real filesystem.

examples.title: A Lifecycle Policy Automating Storage Class Transitions
examples.explanation: This rule applies only to objects whose key starts with `logs/`, and it fully automates a storage-cost curve that matches how log data is actually accessed in practice: recent logs are queried often, so they stay in S3 Standard for the first 30 days; after that, query frequency drops off sharply, so the rule moves them to the cheaper Standard-IA class (accepting a small per-retrieval fee in the rare case someone does query month-old logs); after 90 days, they move again to Glacier, where storage cost drops dramatically further in exchange for retrieval taking minutes to hours if ever needed; and after a full year, `Expiration` permanently deletes them, on the assumption that whatever retention requirement justified keeping them at all has been satisfied by then. None of this requires any application code or manual intervention -- it runs automatically once, based purely on object age, which is exactly the point: automating the tiering means nobody has to remember to do it, and nobody accidentally leaves a year's worth of logs sitting in the most expensive storage class purely because reorganizing them never made it onto anyone's task list.

examples.title: A Bucket Policy That Accidentally Makes Everything Public
examples.explanation: The `Sid` name, 'AllowPartnerRead,' reveals the intent -- someone wanted to grant one specific business partner read access to exported files. But `"Principal": "*"` doesn't mean 'the partner'; it means literally any unauthenticated caller on the internet, so this policy, as written, makes every object in the bucket publicly downloadable by anyone who has or guesses a key. The fixed version replaces the wildcard with a specific AWS account ARN (`111122223333`), which restricts the grant to principals authenticated as that one account -- the partner can still access the objects (assuming they use credentials belonging to that account), but the general public cannot. This exact mistake -- writing `"*"` when the actual intent was 'one known external party' -- is common enough that it's precisely the class of error Block Public Access is designed to catch as a safety net: on an account or bucket where Block Public Access is enabled, this overly broad policy would simply fail to grant the public access it appears to grant, even though the policy document itself is syntactically valid and would otherwise take effect exactly as written.

misconceptions.description: S3 has real folders and directories, so listing or renaming 'a folder' is a cheap, near-instant operation regardless of how many objects it contains.
misconceptions.clarification: S3 has a flat key namespace inside each bucket; what the console displays as folders is a rendering convenience based on shared key prefixes containing `/` characters, not an actual directory structure. Listing by prefix scans and filters keys rather than doing a directory lookup, and there is no atomic rename operation at all -- 'renaming a folder' is implemented as an individual copy-then-delete for every single object that happens to share that prefix, which can be slow and can incur real per-request cost at scale.

misconceptions.description: S3's 'eleven nines of durability' means requests to S3 will essentially never fail.
misconceptions.clarification: Durability (essentially never permanently losing stored data, due to redundant storage across multiple devices and AZs) and availability (the service being reachable and returning successful responses on a given request, published around 99.99% for S3 Standard) are two different guarantees. It's entirely possible for a particular request to fail or time out -- governed by the availability figure -- even though the underlying object data was never at risk of being lost. Application code calling S3 should still include retry logic for transient request failures; that need doesn't go away just because durability is extremely high.

exercises.prompt: An application 'reorganizes' its S3 data nightly by moving all objects under a date-based prefix containing several million keys to a new archive prefix, using a naive per-object copy-then-delete loop in application code. The job has started timing out and its S3 request costs have spiked noticeably. Diagnose why this approach doesn't scale and propose a better strategy.
exercises.code:
# pseudocode for the current nightly job
for key in list_all_objects_under_prefix("data/2026-01-14/"):
    copy_object(from=key, to=key.replace("data/2026-01-14/", "archive/2026-01-14/"))
    delete_object(key)
# runs once per object, sequentially, for several million objects
hints: Recall that S3 has no atomic rename or move operation for a prefix -- what does that imply about the true number of API calls this loop is making?
The loop processes objects one at a time, sequentially -- is there a way to make many of these copy/delete operations happen concurrently instead of strictly one after another?

Consider whether copying every object is even necessary here, given that a lifecycle rule can transition or 'move' objects between prefixes... or whether restructuring key naming to avoid needing bulk moves at all is the more scalable fix.
exercises.solutionCode:
# Better: avoid needing a bulk move at all by naming keys with the archive
# destination baked in from the start, OR at minimum parallelize the copy/delete
# operations instead of running them one at a time, e.g. using S3 Batch Operations
# to issue a single managed job that performs the copy+delete across millions of
# keys with built-in concurrency, retries, and progress tracking.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The fundamental issue is that this job is making two full API calls (one copy, one delete) per object, sequentially, for several million objects -- there is no way to make that fast as a strictly sequential loop, because S3 simply has no bulk-rename primitive to fall back on; the per-object cost the naive loop pays is real, not an artifact of writing the loop poorly. The most scalable fix is S3 Batch Operations, a managed feature specifically built for exactly this class of problem: given a manifest of object keys, it performs a specified operation (like copy) across all of them with built-in parallelism, automatic retries on transient failures, and progress tracking, without the calling application needing to manage a slow sequential loop itself. An even better fix, when it's an option, is avoiding the need for a bulk move altogether -- for instance, writing new data directly under the eventual archive-style key structure from the start, so 'reorganizing' never has to touch millions of pre-existing objects at all. The core lesson is that any design assuming S3 prefixes can be cheaply restructured after the fact is fighting the object-store model rather than working with it.

exercises.prompt: Write an S3 lifecycle rule (JSON) for objects under the 'backups/' prefix: keep them in S3 Standard for the first 14 days (frequent restore testing happens in this window), move them to Standard-IA after that, and permanently delete them after 180 days. Restores after day 180 are never needed.
hints: A Transition entry's 'Days' value is the age at which the transition happens -- you don't need a separate rule for the initial Standard period, since that's simply the default state before any transition fires.
Only one transition is actually needed here, since there are only two storage classes involved (Standard, implicitly, then Standard-IA) -- don't add a Glacier transition that wasn't asked for.
Expiration works the same way as Transitions -- it's just a Days value after which the object is deleted rather than moved.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Objects need no explicit rule for their first 14 days, since S3 Standard is simply where every object starts by default -- the only thing that needs configuring is what happens *after* that. The single `Transitions` entry with `"Days": 14` moves objects to `STANDARD_IA` exactly at that age, matching the requirement that restore testing (which happens in the first 14 days) always finds objects in the faster, no-retrieval-fee Standard class, while older backups shift to cheaper storage since they're accessed far less often. `Expiration` at 180 days permanently deletes the object at that age, matching the stated fact that nothing past day 180 is ever restored -- there's no reason to keep paying for storage (even cheap Standard-IA storage) for data that's already established as never needed again. Adding a Glacier tier here would have been over-engineering relative to what was actually specified: two clearly defined access-pattern phases only need one transition and one expiration, not an additional tier that wasn't asked for.

assessments.prompt: A team observes that an S3 GET request occasionally fails with a transient error, even though they're confident their object was never lost or corrupted. Which statement best explains this?
options: This should be impossible; S3's eleven-nines durability guarantee means requests essentially never fail.

Durability (data not being lost) and availability (the service successfully responding to a given request) are different guarantees; S3's availability target is lower than its durability figure, so occasional transient request failures are expected and should be handled with retry logic.
This indicates the object was stored in a One Zone-IA storage class, which is the only class where transient failures can occur.
This is only possible if the bucket's lifecycle policy has an error in it.
assessments.explanation: Durability and availability are genuinely separate published guarantees -- durability is about not losing the underlying data over time (S3 Standard's famous eleven nines), while availability is about the service reliably responding to any single request right now (published around 99.99% for S3 Standard, a much smaller number of nines). A brief, occasional request failure is consistent with the availability figure and doesn't contradict the durability guarantee at all, which is exactly why option B is correct and option A's premise -- treating durability as if it also covered request success -- is the misconception being tested. Option C incorrectly ties this to a specific storage class (transient request failures aren't a One Zone-IA-specific phenomenon), and option D introduces an unrelated cause (lifecycle policies affect storage class transitions and expiration, not the success rate of GET requests).

assessments.prompt: A developer expects `aws s3 mv s3://bucket/old-prefix/ s3://bucket/new-prefix/ --recursive` on a prefix containing 500,000 objects to complete almost instantly, the way renaming a folder does on a local filesystem. Why is that expectation wrong?
options: The AWS CLI doesn't actually support recursive moves, so this specific command will fail outright.

S3 has no atomic rename operation for a prefix; because S3 is a flat key-value namespace rather than a real directory tree, the CLI must issue an individual CopyObject followed by a DeleteObject for every one of the 500,000 objects -- hundreds of thousands of separate API calls, not one instant metadata change.
The command will in fact complete instantly, because S3 secretly maintains a hidden directory tree beneath what the console displays.
The delay only occurs if Block Public Access happens to be enabled on the bucket.
assessments.explanation: S3's object model is a flat namespace of keys within a bucket -- what looks like a folder is only a shared key prefix, with no underlying directory object that could be renamed as a single operation. The CLI's recursive move is implemented as a copy-then-delete loop over every matching key, so a 500,000-object prefix genuinely becomes roughly a million individual API calls, each with its own latency and cost -- this is real, not a CLI inefficiency that could be optimized away while keeping the same underlying model. Option A is factually wrong (recursive move is supported and will run, just slowly and at real cost), option C invents a hidden directory structure that doesn't exist, and option D introduces Block Public Access, which governs public access grants and has nothing to do with copy/delete latency.

assessments.prompt: While reviewing an older codebase, you find application code that, after every S3 PUT, sleeps briefly and retries a GET in a loop until the new data appears, with a comment saying 'S3 needs a moment to catch up.' What's the most accurate assessment of this code today?
options: It's still necessary -- S3 has always been eventually consistent for all operations and always will be.

It was a legitimate workaround for S3's pre-December-2020 weaker consistency model for overwrite PUTs and deletes, but on modern S3 -- which provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations -- it's no longer needed for consistency reasons, though general retry logic for transient request failures can still be worthwhile.
It indicates the bucket must be using the One Zone-IA storage class, the only class with eventual consistency.
It's actually a workaround for IAM policy propagation delay, unrelated to S3's own consistency model.
assessments.explanation: Before a change AWS shipped in December 2020, S3 offered a weaker consistency model where overwrite PUTs and deletes could, for a brief window, leave a read returning stale or missing data -- exactly the behavior this defensive sleep-and-retry code was written to paper over. Since that change, S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations, meaning a GET immediately after a successful PUT always reflects the latest write, so the specific consistency concern this code guards against no longer exists. Option A misstates S3's current guarantee, option C ties the behavior to a storage class that has nothing to do with read-after-write consistency, and option D introduces IAM propagation, an unrelated AWS behavior entirely separate from S3's own object consistency model. Note that generic retry logic for transient request failures, governed by availability rather than consistency, can still be reasonable to keep -- just not for this stated reason.

assessments.prompt: A colleague proposes storing every uploaded file in S3 Glacier Deep Archive from the moment it's uploaded, reasoning that it's the cheapest storage class and therefore the best default. Explain what's wrong with this reasoning and how you'd actually choose a storage class and lifecycle strategy for a typical file-upload feature.
assessments.modelAnswer: The flaw is treating 'cheapest per-GB storage cost' as the only variable that matters, when storage classes trade that cost against retrieval speed and, for the infrequent-access and archival tiers, an explicit per-retrieval fee. Deep Archive is the cheapest tier specifically because retrieving an object from it can take many hours -- entirely unacceptable for a typical file-upload feature, where a user who uploads a file overwhelmingly expects to be able to view or download it again within seconds, not request a retrieval and wait until the next business day. Choosing a storage class correctly starts from the actual access pattern of the data, not its cost alone: newly uploaded files are almost always accessed frequently in the period right after upload (the user reviewing what they just uploaded, sharing it, or other immediate follow-up actions), so they belong in S3 Standard initially, where there's no retrieval fee and access is instant. As files age, most uploaded-file workloads see a real, predictable drop-off in access frequency -- which is precisely what a lifecycle policy should automate: transition objects to Standard-IA after some observed window of low access (say, 30-60 days, tuned to the actual product's usage data), and only move to Glacier-tier storage for files that are effectively archival and rarely if ever expected to be retrieved again, if that even applies to this particular feature at all. If the actual access pattern per file is hard to predict in advance -- some files stay hot for months, others go cold within days -- S3 Intelligent-Tiering is a reasonable alternative to a fixed, age-based lifecycle rule, since it monitors each object's real access pattern and moves it between tiers automatically rather than relying on a single one-size-fits-all age threshold. The general principle is: design the storage-class strategy around when and how fast the data actually needs to be retrieved, and use cost as the tiebreaker among options that already satisfy that retrieval requirement -- not the other way around.
